quote: Now suppose we discover that a PhD economist buys a lottery ticket every week. We have to ask ourselves: Does this person really understand expected utility, on a gut level? Or have they just been trained to perform certain algebra tricks?
content: The economist has a better answer than the essay allows, and the answer is in the economics literature the essay imagines the economist has merely memorized. Expected utility theory does not say that a two-dollar lottery ticket is irrational; it says it is irrational for an agent whose utility is concave in wealth at every scale, and Rabin’s calibration theorem (Rabin (2000)) shows that any agent who is measurably risk-averse over small stakes must be absurdly risk-averse over large ones, so that small-stakes choices carry almost no information about the agent’s risk attitude. Add that the ticket is a consumption good (a week of anticipation), which economists have modelled since Conlisk (1993), or that the utility of wealth has a convex region (Friedman & Savage (1948), the founding paper on why the same person insures and gambles), and the weekly ticket is consistent with full understanding of the theory. The essay’s diagnostic, then, does not distinguish a person who misunderstands expected utility from a person who understands it better than the diagnostician; and this is the essay’s only worked example of the phenomenon it is alarmed about.

quote: You would probably suspect that the shepherd didn’t understand counting very well.
content: The parable assumes that understanding entails transfer, so that failure to transfer is evidence of rote learning. That assumption is the one the study of transfer refuted. Far transfer, the application of a skill learned in one domain to a superficially different one, is rare and small even in people who demonstrably understand the skill (Barnett & Ceci (2002); Sala & Gobet (2017)); expertise is domain-bound to the point that chess masters’ memory advantage vanishes for random board positions (Chase & Simon 1973), and this is the normal architecture of skill rather than a symptom of miseducation. Scientists who are excellent inside their field and ordinary outside it are therefore what the transfer literature predicts for people who understand their field, not a paradox demanding that we “sit bolt upright in alarm.” The essay could have argued that rationality is a special case in which transfer is achievable with training; instead it argues that failure to transfer proves the skill was never understood, and the evidence on transfer says the inference runs the other way.

quote: And yes, that does make me wonder if I can trust that scientist’s opinions even in their own field—especially when it comes to any controversial issue, any open question, anything that isn’t already nailed down by massive evidence and social convention.
content: This is a testable prediction: religious scientists should be worse scientists, particularly on open questions. No one has found this. About half of American academic scientists report a religious identity and a third believe in God (Ecklund & Scheitle (2007)), and religiosity in that sample is predicted by childhood religion and demographics, not by discipline or productivity; the elite-scientist figures (7% of National Academy members believing in a personal God, Larson & Witham (1998)) show that disbelief correlates with eminence but not that belief predicts error on any scientific question. The historical roll is the awkward part: Faraday was a Sandemanian elder, Maxwell an evangelical Presbyterian, Lemaître a priest who derived the expanding universe from Einstein’s equations and corrected Einstein, Dobzhansky an Orthodox Christian who wrote the founding text of the modern synthesis, Collins the director of the Human Genome Project. The essay would have had to distrust each of them “on any open question,” which is to say on the questions they settled. Compartmentalization is a documented strategy (Ecklund’s interviews find scientists who hold the two domains apart deliberately); the essay is right that it is a strategy and wrong that it is diagnostic of not understanding evidence.

quote: Isaac Newton is justly revered, not for his outdated theory of gravity, but for discovering that—amazingly, surprisingly—the celestial planets, in the glorious heavens, obeyed just the same rules as falling apples.
content: The essay’s hero fails the essay’s test more completely than the spirit-believing scientist it invented. Newton spent more of his working life on alchemy and biblical chronology than on physics, wrote over a million words on theology, dated the Apocalypse, held that the solar system required periodic divine repair, and believed the Trinity a fourth-century corruption (Snobelen (1999); Dobbs, The Janus Faces of Genius, 1991, a book with no DOI). His alchemical notebooks show the same experimental method as the Principia, applied to the transmutation of metals, so the compartment was not even between “the laboratory” and “outside”; it was between two laboratories. By the essay’s inference, Newton “probably never did understand why the scientific rules work” and cannot be trusted on gravitation, an open question in 1687. The historical record is that people who understand the experimental method extremely well have also held beliefs the essay calls wacky, held them for decades, and produced the best science of their era while doing so. That is evidence about how understanding and belief relate in human minds, and the essay’s model of the relationship does not fit it.

quote: (Since there is a trivial isomorphism between graphs and their complements, this profound wisdom conveys exactly the same useful information as a graph with no edges.)
content: A graph and its complement are not isomorphic; the map from a graph to its complement is a bijection on the set of graphs, and self-complementary graphs are rare (the pentagon is one). What the parenthesis means is that the complete graph and the empty graph carry the same information, zero bits, since each is fixed once the vertex count is known. That is right, and the joke lands. But the objection it is used for is misplaced: “everything is connected to everything else,” read as the claim that any two physical systems interact, is not the complete graph on a set of abstract vertices, it is a substantive claim about the world, and it is the claim the essay Universal Fire spent its length defending (“Reality is laced together a lot more tightly than humans might like to believe”). The book asserts universal connectedness in one essay and sneers at it as content-free in the next, and the only difference is who is saying it.
